## Preliminary work

This is an exploratory re-analysis of an existing trial, not a published trial report. Every estimate here is provisional, and the analyses were chosen after the original trial was completed and published. Read the figures as the best current description of what these data support, not as settled findings.
:::

# In brief {.unnumbered}

A randomised trial taught 57 children with Down syndrome a daily one-to-one reading and language programme. Half started immediately; half waited 20 weeks and then received the same programme. This project re-analysed the trial with modern statistical methods to ask three questions: what did the teaching change, how did it work, and what predicts a child's progress?

**What the teaching changed.** After 20 weeks the children who had been taught knew more of what the programme taught them, and read more words:

```{python}
#| echo: false
md(f"""
- **Letter sounds** — the clearest effect in the study: {effect('L')}, {evidence('L')}.
- **Word reading** — {effect('W')}, {evidence('W')}.
- **Taught vocabulary** — the words the programme explicitly taught: {effect('TE')} expressively and {effect('TR')} receptively.
- **Phoneme blending** — {effect('B')}, though this one depends on how the guessing in a three-choice task is modelled.
- **General vocabulary tests** — no detectable change: {effect('R')} receptively, {effect('E')} expressively.
""")
```

**How it seems to work.** Most of the word-reading benefit is attributed to the route through letter-sound knowledge; what remains once letter sounds are accounted for cannot be distinguished from zero.

**What predicts progress.** A child's other test scores describe their current reading level rather well and predict how fast they will move next very poorly. This is the study's most practically important negative result.

**What it cannot tell you.** Only the 20-week comparison is a true experiment. Everything about hearing, speech, memory, vocabulary and dose describes *which children progressed*, not *what would happen if you changed those things*.

# Why this study exists

The trial re-analysed here was set up because of a genuine disagreement about how children with Down syndrome should be taught to read [@burgoyne2012rli]. Children with Down syndrome commonly show relative strengths in visual skills and difficulties with phonological awareness, and recognise more words than they can decode. That profile led some to favour whole-word teaching — which can increase the number of words a child recognises without building the letter-sound route that independent reading rests on. Others argued for phonics, combined with vocabulary teaching, on the grounds that the language difficulties common in Down syndrome would otherwise limit what phonics could achieve. Before this trial the evidence either way came from studies of between 7 and 24 children, with short teaching periods and often no appropriate comparison group.

Two questions follow, and this project takes both seriously. Does such a programme actually help? And can we tell in advance which children will respond, so that scarce one-to-one teaching time is used where it does most good?

# What was done

## The trial

Fifty-seven children with Down syndrome in mainstream primary schools in two UK regions were randomly allocated to one of two groups. The **immediate group** began a reading and language programme straight away. The **waiting group** continued with its usual education, including its usual one-to-one teaching-assistant support, for 20 weeks, and then received the same programme.

The programme was delivered one-to-one by trained teaching assistants in the child's own school, in daily 40-minute sessions, and combined phonics-based reading instruction with explicit vocabulary teaching. Each 20-week block taught a specific set of vocabulary, which was then tested with bespoke measures alongside standardised tests.

Children were assessed four times. The table below is taken from the analysis files rather than from the published design description, because the two differ after the third assessment: teaching did not simply stop.

## The children and the analysis files

```{python}
#| echo: false
head = WORD["headline"]
md(f"""
Of the 57 children randomised, 54 appear in the analysis files: three were lost to follow-up after randomisation. Analyses that need a particular score have slightly fewer again — the word-reading analysis has {head['n_children']} children. At the first assessment the children were about 5 to 10 years old.

Because the analysis starts from the children who are present and have the score in question, the headline estimates are **available-case** estimates. They describe the effect for the children analysed, and they carry the causal reading only if being in the analysis set is unrelated to how a child would have responded. The word-reading section below quantifies exactly how much that assumption matters — and the answer is: enough to take seriously.
""")
```

## What was measured

Most outcomes are test scores of the form "so many correct out of so many items": word reading out of 79 words, letter-sound knowledge out of 32 letters and digraphs, phoneme blending out of 10, nonword reading out of 6, taught vocabulary out of 24, standardised vocabulary out of 170. Two features of such scores matter throughout:

- **They are bounded.** A child cannot score 33 out of 32, and a child near the top of a test has less room to improve than a child in the middle. The models use a distribution designed for "k out of n" counts rather than pretending the scores are unbounded.
- **Some have floors.** On nonword reading and phonetic spelling most children score zero or close to it. A measure on which most children score zero carries very little information about how those children differ, so those two outcomes are analysed as *the chance of moving off the floor* rather than as a score, and are reported separately.

# How the analysis was done, and why

The project uses a deliberate two-step method. Neither step alone answers the questions.

## Step 1 — exploration with machine learning

Gradient-boosting models (LightGBM) were fitted to each outcome to find out which measured characteristics carry information about it, with cross-validation grouped by child so a model is never tested on a child it was trained on. These models are good at finding patterns and bad at telling you what causes what, so they are used for one purpose only: to rank and describe, and to check that the statistical models are not missing something obvious.

Fifty such models were fitted for this report — one for each outcome's level and one for each outcome's change over a period.

## Step 2 — Bayesian statistical models

The scientific estimates come from Bayesian models fitted with PyMC. Bayesian methods were chosen for three reasons that matter in a study this size:

1. **They report uncertainty directly.** With 54 children, uncertainty is the main finding for many outcomes, and it should be visible rather than hidden behind a significance test.
2. **They handle bounded, floored, repeated-measures data** without forcing it into a shape it does not have.
3. **They let a question be asked in more than one way.** The same treatment contrast is estimated by four differently structured model families; agreement across them is evidence that the answer is not an artefact of one modelling choice.

```{python}
#| echo: false
md(f"""
This report draws on **{RELEASE['n_fits_trial']} fitted statistical models of this trial**, all refitted together so that every number comes from one consistent run of the same code against the same data. (The project also maintains {RELEASE['n_fits_other_cohort']} models of a separate, older observational cohort, which this report does not cover.)
""")
```

Which covariates each model adjusts for was decided in advance from a causal diagram of how the skills are believed to relate, not by choosing whichever variables improved the fit. That choice makes the *treatment* estimate as clean as possible, and it is one of the reasons the other coefficients in those models should not be read as effects in their own right.

## How to read the numbers

There are no p-values here. Each estimate is reported as:

- a **median** — the single most representative value;
- an **89% credible range** — a range containing the true value with 89% probability, given the model and the data. (89% rather than the conventional 95% deliberately: 95% is an arbitrary inheritance from significance testing, and the extreme ends of a simulated range are its least stable part.)
- a **direction probability, P** — the probability the effect goes the way the estimate says.

The project attaches fixed words to those probabilities so that different documents mean the same thing:

| P | Label |
| --- | --- |
| 0.75 or more | suggestive |
| 0.91 or more | moderate |
| 0.97 or more | strong |
| 0.99 or more | very strong |
| below 0.75 | inconclusive |

Three cautions about those labels. They describe **how sure the direction is, not how big the effect is** — "strong evidence the programme helps" says nothing about whether the help is large enough to matter in a classroom. A flat result is **inconclusive**, which means the study could not tell; it never means "no effect". And where it matters, this report also gives the probability that a benefit is at least as large as a value the project agreed would matter in practice.

## What counts as caused, and what does not

This is the most important distinction in the report, and it is applied without exception.

**Causal:** the t2 comparison between the randomly assigned groups. This is the only place randomisation is doing its work.

**Associational:** everything else. Every relationship between one skill and another, every coefficient on age, hearing, speech, memory or ability, and every dose-response slope. These describe *which children progressed*, not *which levers move outcomes*. Reading a covariate coefficient from a model built to estimate a treatment effect as though it were itself causal is a well-documented error, and this report does not do it.

## Checks every result had to pass

Each model is fitted by simulation, and simulation can fail quietly. Before any number reaches this report, a fit must show that its independent simulation runs agreed with each other, that it drew enough effectively independent samples, and that it produced **no divergences** — a specific warning that the simulation may have missed part of the answer. A fit also has to demonstrate that any sensitivity analysis its result depends on actually ran.

```{python}
#| echo: false
statuses = RELEASE["statuses"]
withheld = RELEASE["withheld"]
md(f"""
In this run **{statuses.get('ok', 0)} of {RELEASE['n_fits']} fits passed every check**, and not one has a single divergence. {len(withheld)} results are withheld, {RELEASE['n_withheld_other_cohort']} of them from the separate historical cohort — a withheld result is one we are **declining to state**, not one that found nothing. Nothing in this report is withheld.
""")
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Phoneme blending depends on how guessing is modelled

The blending test asks the child to pick one of three pictures, so a child who understands nothing still scores about a third of the items by chance. The project therefore requires two models to be reported together: an ordinary one, and one that explicitly allows for the guessing floor.

```{python}
#| echo: false
pair = RESULTS.get("blending_link") or []
names = {"logit": "Ordinary model", "three_choice_guessing_floor": "Guessing-floor model"}
if pair:
    header = "| Model | Effect (items of 10) | 89% range | P(>0) | P(at least 1 item) |\n| --- | ---: | :---: | ---: | ---: |\n"
    body = "\n".join(
        f"| {names.get(str(r['link']), r['link'])} | {n(r['median'])} | {n(r['lo'])} to {n(r['hi'])} | "
        f"{prob(r['prob_pos'])} | {r['prob_meaningful']:.2f} |"
        for r in pair
    )
    delta = pair[0].get("elpd_difference")
    delta_se = pair[0].get("elpd_difference_se")
    tail = ""
    if delta is not None and delta_se is not None:
        tail = (
            f"\n\nThe data do not decide between the two: the difference in predictive fit is "
            f"{n(delta)} ± {n(delta_se, sign=False)}, which is well inside noise. So the honest "
            "statement is that blending improved, and that how much depends on an assumption the data cannot settle."
        )
    md(header + body + tail)
```
:::

## Direction is not size

A result can be almost certainly positive and still be too small to matter. The project therefore also asks, for each outcome, how probable it is that the benefit reaches a size agreed to be practically meaningful.

```{python}
#| echo: false
rows = [r for r in RESULTS["itt_suite"] if r.get("prob_benefit_ge_delta") is not None and not r["floor_rule"]]
rows = sorted(rows, key=lambda r: -(r["prob_benefit_ge_delta"] or 0))[:8]
header = "| Outcome | Difference that would matter | Probability the benefit is at least that big |\n| --- | ---: | ---: |\n"
md(header + "\n".join(
    f"| {label(r['symbol'])} | {n(r['delta'], 0, sign=False)} {unit(r['symbol'], r['delta'])} | "
    f"{r['prob_benefit_ge_delta']:.2f} |"
    for r in rows
))
```

Letter sounds and word reading are the two outcomes where a clearly positive effect and a probably-worthwhile one coincide: for both, the probability that the benefit reaches the agreed threshold is around 0.9. For taught vocabulary the direction is clear but the practical size is not. For blending and expressive grammar it is close to a coin toss whether the benefit reaches one item.

::: {.callout-warning}
These practical-difference thresholds were set after the first results were reviewed, so for this analysis round they are a transparent post-hoc judgement rather than a rule fixed in advance. The rule behind them — half the waiting group's own natural gain over the untaught period, with a floor of one item — has since been adopted as the project's standing rule, so future rounds will apply it prospectively.
:::

## The same answer from differently built models

A single model's answer can be an artefact of its structure. The randomised 20-week contrast was therefore estimated several ways. Three of them put the effect on the same items scale and are compared directly below: the headline model (one row per child at the 20-week assessment, adjusted for the child's own baseline score and age); an arm-by-wave model of the whole trajectory; and a model that stacks every period's post-score given its pre-score. A fourth, which models the score at each timepoint without a baseline covariate, is discussed after them.

```{python}
#| echo: false
triangulation_table(["L", "W", "TE", "TR", "F"])
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
tri = {row["symbol"]: row for row in RESULTS["triangulation"]}
agree = [s for s, row in tri.items() if row.get("consistent")]
disagree = [s for s, row in tri.items() if not row.get("consistent")]
md(f"""
The comparison carries its own verdict on whether the designs agree — in direction and in whether their ranges overlap. {len(agree)} of the {len(tri)} outcomes it covers are consistent across all three. """
   + (f"""The exception is {", ".join(label(s).lower() for s in disagree)}, where the three designs do not even agree on the sign."""
      if disagree else "There is no exception.")
)
```

The fourth view is a model of the score at each timepoint, with no baseline covariate. It reproduces the same ordering, but for the two standardised vocabulary tests it leans negative where the others sit near zero. That is a known consequence of its structure rather than a sign of harm: with no baseline score in the model, a chance difference between the groups at the start passes straight through into the later contrast — and for receptive vocabulary this study's groups did start slightly apart. It is reported because leaving it out would be selective, not because it changes the conclusion.

One of the three deserves an explicit caveat, because agreement can be misread as independent confirmation. The arm-by-wave model's word-reading estimate leans on an assumption built into it before it saw the data — how large an effect it was prepared to expect:

```{python}
#| echo: false
grid = (RESULTS.get("prior_dependence") or {}).get("lrp-rli-did-001")
if grid:
    header = "| How wide the model's prior expectation was | Estimate | 89% range | P(>0) |\n| --- | ---: | :---: | ---: |\n"
    md(header + "\n".join(
        f"| prior SD {c['prior_sd']:.2f} | {n(c['items'])} words | {n(c['lo'])} to {n(c['hi'])} | {prob(c['prob_direction'])} |"
        for c in grid["cells"]
    ))
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
if grid:
    lo_cell, hi_cell = grid["cells"][0], grid["cells"][-1]
    md(f"""
Across that range the estimate moves from {n(lo_cell['items'])} to {n(hi_cell['items'])} words and every range spans zero, while the direction stays positive throughout. What this model contributes is therefore **corroboration of the direction, not a second measurement of the size** — and the report treats it that way. Nor are these independent experiments: they are different ways of modelling the same 20-week comparison in the same children, so agreement between them rules out a modelling artefact, not a mistake in the data.
""")
```

## The assumption it does not survive

Four of the 57 randomised children have no word-reading score at the 20-week assessment: three were lost to follow-up after randomisation and one was assessed but has no score. That is a small number, and it is enough to matter.

```{python}
#| echo: false
figure("word_reading_envelope", "The headline estimate, three analyses that make different assumptions about the missing scores, and the shaded band showing what is arithmetically possible if the missing children took the most extreme scores available to them.")
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
bounds = WORD.get("attrition_bounds") or {}
grid = WORD.get("missingness_delta_grid") or {}
md(f"""
Under assumptions most researchers would accept — that whether a score is missing does not depend on what the score would have been, once the child's group, screening reading and age are taken into account — the estimate stays positive and close to two words. Across a grid of {grid.get('n_cells', 0)} alternative assumptions about how the missing children would have scored, the estimate ranges from {n(grid.get('median_min'))} to {n(grid.get('median_max'))} words.

But if you make no assumption at all, and simply ask what is arithmetically possible, the four missing scores could place the true difference anywhere between **{n(bounds.get('worst_case_items_lower'))} and {n(bounds.get('worst_case_items_upper'))} words**. That range includes a substantial negative value. It is not a plausible scenario — it requires every missing child to take the most extreme score available — but it is the honest bound, and the headline should never be quoted without it.
""")
```

## How the effect appears to arise

If the programme improved word reading, what did it improve *first*? The models decompose the word-reading difference into a part that runs through a candidate skill and a part that does not.

```{python}
#| echo: false
figure("mediation_routes", "The 20-week word-reading difference split into the part attributed to each candidate route and the part attributed to everything else. The thin line is the 89% range of the part running through the route. Each row is a separate model fitted to its own set of children, so the row totals are not directly comparable with one another.")
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
med = RESULTS.get("mediation") or []


def _cell(entry, key):
    part = entry.get(key)
    if not part:
        return "—"
    return f"{n(part['median'])} [{n(part['lo'])}, {n(part['hi'])}]"


header = (
    "| Route tested | Total difference | Through this route | Not through this route |\n"
    "| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |\n"
)
md(header + "\n".join(
    f"| {e['route']} | {_cell(e, 'total')} | **{_cell(e, 'through_route')}** | {_cell(e, 'not_through_route')} |"
    for e in med
))
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
letters = next((e for e in med if e["route"].startswith("Letter-sound")), None)
if letters:
    through, direct = letters["through_route"], letters["not_through_route"]
    md(f"""
Read the letter-sound row carefully. Of a total difference of {n(letters['total']['median'])} words, {n(through['median'])} words (89% range {n(through['lo'])} to {n(through['hi'])}, P = {prob(through['prob_pos'])}) is attributed to the route through letter-sound knowledge, and {n(direct['median'])} words (89% range {n(direct['lo'])} to {n(direct['hi'])}) to everything else. The second number is small, but its range is wide: the data are consistent with a modest additional route, and equally consistent with none. The right summary is that **the letter-sound route accounts for most of the estimated benefit, and what remains cannot be distinguished from zero** — not that nothing else contributes.

The negative control matters here too. A mediation model that finds a route through *any* skill you put into it is not telling you anything. Expressive grammar — which the programme did not target and which has no plausible role in decoding printed words within 20 weeks — was run through the same machinery and returned essentially nothing through its route, which is the behaviour that makes the letter-sound result worth attending to.
""")
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Why mediation deserves more caution than the headline

The 20-week comparison is protected by randomisation. This decomposition is not: it asks what would have happened had the children's letter-sound knowledge been set to particular values, which no one randomised. It assumes there is no unmeasured characteristic that raises both letter-sound knowledge and word reading, and that assumption cannot be tested with these data. Treat it as the best available account of *how* the effect arose, not as a second experimental result.
:::

# What predicts progress {#sec-predictors}

This is the question teachers ask most often, and it has the least comfortable answer.

## Where a child is, versus how fast they move

```{python}
#| echo: false
figure("gb_predictability", "How much of each outcome the exploratory models account for in children they were not trained on. Each dot is one model; the bar is the median. Left: a child's current score from their other scores at the same assessment. Right: the change over the following period, from what is known now.")
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
perf = pd.DataFrame(RESULTS["gb"]["performance"]).dropna(subset=["pooled_r2"])
levels = perf[perf["kind"] == "level"]["pooled_r2"]
gains = perf[perf["kind"] == "gain"]["pooled_r2"]
md(f"""
The two sets of models ask different questions, and the difference matters.

The **level** models describe a child's score using their *other scores from the same assessment*. Across {len(levels)} such models the median explained variation, in children the model had never seen, is {levels.median():.2f}. That is a description of how these skills hang together at one moment, not a prediction of the future — and part of it is simply that all the measures were taken from the same child on the same day.

The **change** models are genuinely predictive: they use what is known about a child *now* to predict how much they will gain over the *next* period. Across {len(gains)} such models the median is {gains.median():.2f}, and for word reading it is {perf[perf['model_id'] == 'lrp-rli-gbg-012']['pooled_r2'].iloc[0]:.2f}.

That contrast is the finding. **A child's profile of scores describes where their reading is now rather well, and tells you very little about how fast it will move next.** Some of that is measurement — a change score subtracts two noisy numbers and keeps both lots of noise — but it should temper any expectation that a test profile can identify in advance which children will respond best to teaching.
""")
```

## Which measures carry the information

```{python}
#| echo: false
figure("gb_ranking_word_reading_level", "What the exploratory model leans on when predicting a child's word-reading level.")
```

The measures that predict a child's word-reading level are the ones a teacher would guess: letter-sound knowledge and early spelling, then the other reading measures. This is closer to a description of how these skills hang together than a discovery, and it should be read that way.

## Do the two methods agree?

The project's two steps rank predictors by completely different machinery — one by how much a tree ensemble's accuracy degrades when a variable is shuffled, the other by a Bayesian model that shrinks unimportant coefficients towards zero. Where they agree, the ranking is likely to reflect something in the data rather than one method's quirks.

```{python}
#| echo: false
agree = RESULTS.get("ranking_agreement") or []
if agree:
    header = (
        "| Outcome | Quantity ranked | Constructs compared | Rank agreement (Spearman) |\n"
        "| --- | --- | ---: | ---: |\n"
    )
    md(header + "\n".join(
        f"| {row['outcome']} | {row['quantity']} | {row['n_shared_constructs']} | {row['spearman_rho']:+.2f} |"
        for row in agree
    ))
else:
    md("*Ranking agreement pending.*")
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
if agree:
    lvl = [r for r in agree if r["quantity"] == "level"]
    chg = [r for r in agree if r["quantity"] != "level"]
    md(f"""
The two methods agree moderately about **levels** (rank correlations of {" and ".join(f"{r['spearman_rho']:+.2f}" for r in lvl)}) and much less about **change** ({" and ".join(f"{r['spearman_rho']:+.2f}" for r in chg)}). For letter-sound change they agree not at all.

That is the same finding as the previous section arriving from a different direction. When a target carries little predictable signal, two honest methods will rank the noise differently — so a published "top predictors of progress" list built from one method on data like these would be largely irreproducible.
""")
```

## Which earlier skills track later reading

```{python}
#| echo: false
figure("mechanism_forest", "How strongly each earlier skill tracks later word reading, per standard deviation, adjusted for the model's covariate set. These are associations.")
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
items = (RESULTS.get("mechanism") or {}).get("items_scale") or []
by_label = {row["label"]: row for row in items}
ls = by_label.get("Letter-sound knowledge")
if ls:
    md(f"""
Letter-sound knowledge is the strongest of these. On its own item scale, comparing a child at the lowest observed letter-sound score with one at the highest ({n(ls['exposure_low'], 0, sign=False)} versus {n(ls['exposure_high'], 0, sign=False)} of 32), the model puts about {n(ls['items_median'])} words of 79 between them at the end of a period (89% range {n(ls['items_lo'])} to {n(ls['items_hi'])}), holding the rest of the model's covariates at the fitted children's values.

This is an association, and the qualification is not a formality: children who know more letter sounds differ from children who know fewer in many ways this study did not measure. What the trial *does* establish causally is that the programme raised letter-sound knowledge, and the mediation analysis says the word-reading benefit ran through it. Those two facts together make letter sounds the most promising target this study identifies — but "promising target" is weaker than "proven lever", and the difference is real.
""")
```

## Comparing children, and following one child

A subtle point with real consequences for teaching. When a study reports that "children with better speech read more words", that can mean two different things: that children who articulate more clearly are, as a group, further ahead than children who do not; or that when a particular child's speech improves, that child's reading improves too. The first is a statement about differences between children; the second is about change within a child. They can point in different directions, and only the second resembles something a teacher could act on.

```{python}
#| echo: false
pooled = RESULTS.get("pooled_levels") or []
if pooled:
    header = "| Model | Predictor | Comparing children | Within the same child |\n| --- | --- | ---: | ---: |\n"
    lines = []
    for entry in pooled:
        between = entry.get("between") or {}
        within = entry.get("within") or {}
        if not between and not within:
            continue
        lines.append(
            f"| `{entry['model_id'].replace('lrp-rli-', '')}` | {entry.get('predictor_label', entry.get('mechanism_symbol'))} | "
            f"{n(between.get('median'))} [{n(between.get('lo'))}, {n(between.get('hi'))}] | "
            f"{n(within.get('median'))} [{n(within.get('lo'))}, {n(within.get('hi'))}] |"
        )
    md(header + "\n".join(lines) if lines else "*Between/within results pending.*")
else:
    md("*Between/within results pending.*")
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
figure("pooled_levels_between_within", "The same association estimated two ways for each predictor: comparing one child with another, and following one child from one assessment to the next. Positive means more of the predictor goes with more reading.")
```

These models separate the two deliberately, and the separation is the point: the between-child part and the within-child part are not the same number, so a single coefficient that blends them — which is what a naive analysis of repeated measures reports — is not a quantity anyone can interpret.

# Hearing and speech {#sec-hearing-speech}

Two child characteristics come up constantly in practice, and the study can say something about both — but less than a teacher would like, and not in the direction one might expect.

```{python}
#| echo: false
hs = RESULTS.get("hearing_speech") or {}
gain = (hs.get("whole_study_gain") or {})
hearing = gain.get("hs")
speech = gain.get("deapp_c")
if hearing:
    md(f"""
**Hearing.** The study carries a single baseline flag: 1 if the child had impaired hearing *or* a history of repeated ear infections, 0 if both were clear. Children carrying that flag gained, if anything, **more** words over the study than children without it ({n(hearing['words_median'])} words per standard deviation of the flag, 89% range {n(hearing['words_lo'])} to {n(hearing['words_hi'])}, P = {prob(hearing['prob_pos'])}), and the same direction appears in several other models.

This is reported because it is consistent and counter-intuitive, not because it is believed. It does **not** mean hearing difficulty helps reading. The flag is coarse: it merges a hearing impairment with a history of ear infections, it was recorded once at baseline so it cannot track fluctuating conductive hearing loss, and it is unknown for nine of the 54 children. The most likely explanations are chance in a sample of about fifty children, or the flag standing in for something else — which children were being monitored or supported more closely, for instance. And crucially, every model that carries this coefficient included it to clean up some *other* estimate; none was designed to estimate hearing's own association, and reading it as though it were is precisely the error this report warns about elsewhere.
""")
if speech:
    md(f"""
**Speech clarity.** Children whose speech is more accurate read more words at any given moment, and the association with decoding nonwords is stronger still. But once a child's own earlier reading score is in the model, the association with *further gains* is small, and as a baseline predictor of the whole study's gain it is absent ({n(speech['words_median'])} words per standard deviation, 89% range {n(speech['words_lo'])} to {n(speech['words_hi'])}). That is the profile of a stable between-child correlate — children who articulate more accurately are further along the same alphabetic path — rather than of something that changes the rate of progress.

One measurement caveat travels with every speech number here: the score is a trial-era scoring of a picture-naming task that is more lenient than the published re-scoring of this same cohort, so it is a relative accuracy scale rather than an absolute one.
""")
```

**Did the programme work less well for children with hearing difficulty or less clear speech?** That is the question practice most wants answered, and this trial is too small to settle it.

```{python}
#| echo: false
subgroups = (RESULTS.get("hearing_speech") or {}).get("randomised_window_by_subgroup") or []
if subgroups:
    header = (
        "| Children | Taught group | Waiting group | Difference |\n"
        "| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |\n"
    )
    md(header + "\n".join(
        f"| {row['subgroup']} | {row['mean_gain_immediate']:.1f} words (n = {row['n_immediate']}) | "
        f"{row['mean_gain_waiting']:.1f} words (n = {row['n_waiting']}) | {n(row['difference'])} |"
        for row in subgroups
    ))
```

These are **plain averages of the observed gains over the randomised 20 weeks**, not model estimates, and the groups behind them contain between about seven and sixteen children each. Read them only as an absence of any visible warning sign: the gap between taught and waiting children is, if anything, slightly larger among children flagged for hearing difficulty and among those with less clear speech. With this many children a difference large enough to matter in either direction would be invisible, so the honest answer is "no indication of a problem, and nowhere near enough data to rule one out". No subgroup treatment effect is estimated anywhere in this project, deliberately.

# What this study cannot tell you

- **Whether the programme works for children unlike these.** Fifty-seven children recruited in 2009 in two UK regions, in mainstream primary schools with existing teaching-assistant support. Nothing here establishes what happens in different settings or at different ages.
- **What the long-term outcome is.** The randomised comparison covers 20 weeks. What happens over years is not addressed.
- **Whether changing a predictor would change an outcome.** Hearing, speech clarity, phonological memory and vocabulary all track reading progress in these data. None of those relationships is an experiment, and none of them licenses an intervention.
- **How much of the effect would survive in ordinary practice.** The programme was delivered daily, one-to-one, by trained staff, with fidelity monitoring. That is the intervention that was tested.
- **Anything about children who were not assessed.** The missing-data envelope in @sec-word-reading is the honest statement of that limit.

# What this means for teaching

These implications follow from the results above; where one rests on an association rather than the experiment, that is said explicitly.

**Teach letter sounds explicitly, and expect them to move.** This is the clearest experimental result in the study, and it is also the outcome most likely to have moved by an amount that matters: the probability the gain reaches the project's own practical threshold is the highest of any outcome measured.

**Expect word reading to follow letter sounds, not to precede them.** The mediation analysis attributes most of the reading benefit to the letter-sound route. If letter sounds are not moving, the reading gain this programme produces is unlikely to appear.

**Teach vocabulary explicitly if you want taught vocabulary to improve — and do not expect a standardised vocabulary score to move in 20 weeks.** The programme reliably taught the words it taught. Generalisation beyond them is at best a lean in these data, and standardised tests did not shift.

**Do not use a test profile to decide who gets taught.** The models describe a child's current level reasonably well and predict their rate of progress poorly. There is no defensible way, on this evidence, to identify in advance the children who will not benefit.

**Treat dose observationally.** Children who attended more sessions progressed more, but children who attend more differ from children who attend less in ways this study cannot untangle. That finding describes attendance; it does not establish that adding sessions adds progress.

# What this means for research

**The two-step method earned its keep, in one direction.** The exploratory models did not surface predictors the causal models had missed; what they added was the level-versus-change contrast, which is a substantive result rather than a methodological aside.

**Change is hard to predict, and that deserves direct attention.** A field that routinely reports predictors of *level* while implying predictors of *progress* should confront how weak the second is. Measurement error in change scores is part of it, and better-designed change measures would help.

**The floors are a measurement problem, not a statistical one.** Nonword reading (6 items) and phonetic spelling produce floors so severe that the analysis has to change the question to "did the child move off the floor at all". Instruments with usable range at the bottom would recover real information here.

**Missing outcomes deserve the treatment given here as standard.** Four missing scores in a 57-child trial are enough to move a headline result from clearly positive to arithmetically ambiguous. Reporting the assumption envelope alongside the estimate should be routine, not exceptional.

**The obvious next experiments follow from the mediation result.** If the reading benefit runs through letter-sound knowledge, then the questions worth randomising next are about that route: how much letter-sound instruction is enough, whether the same route operates for children who begin with none, and whether the vocabulary component earns its place in the programme at all.

Every number in this report is generated from the fitted models rather than typed in, and each carries a model identifier so it can be traced to one fit. The per-model pages hold the full specification, priors, diagnostics and sensitivity analyses for each of the {RELEASE['n_fits']} statistical fits; the family notes explain what each family of models can and cannot support; and `METHODS.md` records the conventions.

All {RELEASE['n_fits']} statistical models — {RELEASE['n_fits_trial']} of this trial and {RELEASE['n_fits_other_cohort']} of a separate historical cohort — and the {len(RESULTS['gb']['performance'])} exploratory models were refitted together in one sweep, from one version of the code and one version of the data, at the project's full sampling settings. {statuses.get('ok', 0)} passed every check. The {sum(v for k, v in statuses.items() if k != 'ok')} withheld all belong to that other cohort, and all for the same reason: a test's maximum possible score has never been confirmed from its manual, so a model that needs to know it cannot be published. That is a documentation gap rather than a statistical one.
""")

## Reproducibility

The figures and every quoted quantity are produced by `scripts/build_summary_report.py` from the stored model output, and each fit records the code commit, the data checksum and the environment it ran in. Re-running the sweep and this report regenerates the document; if a number here disagrees with a model page, the model page is the source.
